questions.question: What are the routing capabilities of Go's http.ServeMux, and when would you use a third-party router?
questions.title: Http Router Basics
questions.direct_answer: ServeMux: exact paths, prefix subtrees (trailing slash), Go 1.22+ adds methods and path params ({id}). Use ServeMux until you need middleware chains, route groups, or complex matching — then chi/gin/echo.

sections.title: Quick Revision
sections.content: ServeMux: exact paths, prefix subtrees (trailing slash), Go 1.22+ adds methods and path params ({id}). Use ServeMux until you need middleware chains, route groups, or complex matching — then chi/gin/echo.

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
ServeMux's three generations of capability:

Pre-1.22: exact + prefix
```go
mux.HandleFunc("/api/users", h)     // exact
mux.HandleFunc("/static/", h)      // subtree
mux.HandleFunc("/", h)              // catch-all
```

Go 1.22+: methods + path parameters
```go
mux.HandleFunc("GET /users/{id}", getUser)   // method + param
mux.HandleFunc("POST /users", createUser)
// r.PathValue("id") — the extracted parameter
```

What ServeMux still doesn't have — where third-party routers win:
1. Middleware chains (chi's r.Use(logging, auth)) — composable, per-route
2. Route groups (chi's r.Route("/api", ...))
3. Complex matching (regex constraints, host matching)
4. Route introspection (for docs generation, auth maps)

The decision: ServeMux for most services (1.22+ covers the common API shape: method + path + param); chi when middleware composition is the priority; gin/echo for the full framework (their ecosystems, their conventions).

The verification pattern: whatever router you choose, the handler signature stays func(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) — the http.Handler interface is the universal contract, and middleware is func(http.Handler) http.Handler — the patterns compose across routers.

sections.title: Mental Model
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart TD
    MUX[ServeMux 1.22+] --> M[method + path + param]
    MUX --> E[exact match first]
    MUX --> P[longest prefix subtree]
    CHI[chi router] --> MW[middleware chains]
    GIN[gin framework] --> CTX[gin.Context]
```

sections.title: Deep Dive
sections.content:
The 1.22 ServeMux restructure, mechanically: patterns became (method, path, params) — the matcher indexes by method+path-prefix, extracts named segments ({id} from /users/{id}) into r.PathValue, and handles the conflicts at registration time (overlapping patterns are now a compile-time-style error at startup — registering both /users/{id} and /users/x panics or errors, catching ambiguity the old mux silently resolved by longest-prefix).

The middleware difference, which is the real third-party value: Go's middleware pattern is a function wrapping an http.Handler: func(next http.Handler) http.Handler — any router can do this, but chi's r.Use() composes the chain at registration (readable, per-route scoping), while net/http's approach requires manual wrapping (func myMiddleware(next http.HandlerFunc) http.HandlerFunc { ... } and wrapping each handler or the mux itself). The pattern is identical; the ergonomics differ.

The lock-in question, which interviews use to test judgment: the http.Handler interface is the standard — handlers written against it work with every router (ServeMux, chi, gin with an adapter). Write handlers as http.HandlerFunc, keep the router a thin dispatch layer, and switching costs a routing file, not a rewrite.
